title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
summary: The single lens for diagnosing model error: tell underfitting from overfitting on sight, and know which lever fixes which.

slides.subTitle: Bias vs. variance, defined
slides.markdown:
A model's total error splits into two parts you can influence. **Bias** is error from oversimplified assumptions — a straight line fit to a curved trend — so the model **underfits**: wrong the same way on training and new data alike. **Variance** is error from over-sensitivity to the training sample — the model **overfits**, learning noise that won't repeat.

A linear regression on a curved relationship has high bias, low variance. A deep, unpruned tree on 50 rows has low bias, high variance. You rarely kill both at once.

slides.subTitle: The decomposition
slides.markdown:
Expected test error decomposes into three additive terms: **bias²** + **variance** + **irreducible error** (noise no model can remove). As model complexity rises, bias² falls but variance rises — total error traces a **U-shape**, bottoming out at a sweet spot before variance takes over.

![Total error decomposing into bias squared, variance, and irreducible error against model complexity](assets/bias-variance-decomposition.svg)

assets.alt: Total error decomposing into bias squared, variance, and irreducible error against model complexity

slides.subTitle: High bias in practice
slides.markdown:
High bias shows up as a model that's bad everywhere — **both training and validation error are high, and close to each other**. A linear model predicting house prices from only square footage might sit at 20% error on training data and 21% on validation: it hasn't even learned the training set well, so there's no gap to close.

The tell isn't a gap — it's the training error itself being unacceptably high. Fixing this means giving the model more capacity to represent the pattern, not tuning it harder.

slides.subTitle: High variance in practice
slides.markdown:
High variance shows up as a large **gap** between low training error and much higher validation error. A 15-feature polynomial fit to 30 noisy points might hit 2% training error but 35% validation error — it memorized the specific points instead of the underlying trend.

The tell is the gap itself: the model clearly *can* fit data well, it just isn't fitting the right thing. Fixing this means constraining the model or giving it more data to generalize from, not more capacity.

slides.subTitle: Reading learning curves
slides.markdown:
Plot training and validation error against training-set size. **High bias**: both curves converge quickly to a high, similar error — more data won't help. **High variance**: a persistent gap between a low training curve and a higher validation curve that's still narrowing as data grows — more data helps here.

![Learning curves showing training and validation error versus training-set size](assets/learning-curves.svg)

assets.alt: Learning curves showing training and validation error versus training-set size

slides.subTitle: The three levers
slides.markdown:
Three levers shift where you sit on the curve. **Model complexity** — more parameters or depth lowers bias but raises variance, and vice versa. **Training data size** — more data lowers variance without touching bias, because a bigger sample generalizes better without changing what the model can represent. **Regularization** — penalties like L2 or pruning trade a little bias for a lot less variance by discouraging the model from chasing noise.

None of these levers is free — each is a deliberate trade, not a fix.

slides.subTitle: Different, sometimes opposite, playbooks
slides.markdown:
High bias and high variance need opposite fixes — applying the wrong one wastes time or makes things worse.

| Lever | High bias fix | High variance fix |
|---|---|---|
| Model capacity | Increase (deeper tree, more features) | Decrease (prune, fewer features) |
| Training data | Won't help much | Add more |
| Regularization | Reduce | Increase |
| Ensembling | Boosting (reduces bias) | Bagging (reduces variance) |

Diagnose from the train/validation gap first — the fix for one symptom actively hurts the other.

slides.subTitle: Data can't fix a bias problem
slides.markdown:
A team sees poor accuracy and reaches for the default fix: collect more training data. If the real problem is **high bias** — a model too simple to represent the pattern — more data changes nothing, because the ceiling is the model's capacity, not the sample size. Training and validation error stay high and close together no matter how much data you add.

Check the diagnosis first: a shrinking gap with more data signals variance; a flat, high floor signals bias, and the fix there is a more expressive model or better features, not a bigger dataset.

slides.sectionTitle: Why ensembles target one side of the trade-off
slides.subTitle: Bagging vs boosting, mechanically
slides.markdown:
**Bagging** (random forests) trains many high-variance models (deep, unpruned trees) on different bootstrap samples and averages their predictions — averaging cancels out each tree's idiosyncratic noise, so variance drops sharply while each individual tree's bias is untouched. That's why bagging is the standard fix for a high-variance base model.

**Boosting** (gradient boosting) does the opposite: it trains a sequence of weak, high-bias learners, each one correcting the previous ensemble's residual errors, progressively reducing bias. This is exactly why the ensembling row in the earlier compare table pairs boosting with bias and bagging with variance — the mechanism, not just convention, determines which side of the trade-off each technique moves.
